opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today's Gospel from Matthew 13:44–52 asks a simple question with an answer that is anything but simple: **What is the Kingdom of God worth to me?**

Jesus tells a series of short parables that, together, reveal the answer.

First, He speaks of a man who unexpectedly discovers a treasure hidden in a field. Filled with joy, the man sells everything he owns to purchase that field. It is important to notice that he does not give everything away reluctantly. He does so joyfully because he understands that what he is gaining is far greater than what he is leaving behind.

Jesus then tells of a merchant who has spent his life searching for fine pearls. When he finally discovers one pearl of extraordinary value, he too sells everything to possess it. Unlike the first man, this merchant has been searching all along. One found the treasure unexpectedly; the other found it after a lifetime of seeking. Yet both arrive at the same conclusion: nothing compares to the Kingdom of God.

These two parables remind me that people come to Christ in different ways. Some encounter Him unexpectedly through an experience or a person. Others spend years searching for meaning before finally discovering Him. Regardless of how we arrive, the invitation is the same. Once we recognize the incomparable value of God's Kingdom, everything else begins to find its proper place.

Jesus then shifts to the image of a fishing net gathering every kind of fish. Only after the net is full are the fish separated. This reminds me that God is patient. He allows good and evil to exist together for a time, leaving judgment to Himself rather than to us. It is a humbling reminder that I am called to remain faithful, not to decide who belongs to God.

Finally, Jesus speaks of the householder who brings from his storeroom both the old and the new. Christ does not discard the Old Testament; rather, it is fulfilled in Him. The wisdom of Solomon, the Law, and the prophets all point toward Jesus. Through Christ, what once seemed incomplete is now fully revealed.

As I reflect on today's Gospel alongside Solomon's prayer for wisdom, I notice how beautifully they complement one another. Solomon could have asked for wealth, success, or power, yet he asked for an understanding heart so he could faithfully lead God's people. Jesus now reveals that the greatest treasure is not found in earthly success but in the Kingdom of God itself.

The Psalm gives words to the prayer I want to make my own: **"Every false way I hate. Lord, direct me."** I often think of "false ways" as the faults of others, yet the Psalm gently turns my attention inward. It invites me to ask God to reveal the false ways within my own heart—my pride, my impatience, my fears, and my desire to control what I cannot.

Perhaps this is the wisdom Solomon sought: not merely the ability to make good decisions, but a heart willing to let God continually reshape it. If Christ truly is the greatest treasure, then allowing Him to transform my heart is not a sacrifice to be endured but a joy to be embraced.
